text: Sunt et alia quamplurima animalia, que, quanquam infra septa foreste uiuunt{1} et oneri{2} et cure mediocrium{f:a}{3} subiacent, foreste tamen nequaquam censeri possunt{4}, qualia sunt{5} equi{f:b}{6}, bubali{f:c}{7}, uacce et similia.

f:b: Gestüte im Forst kennen die Pipe rolls seit 1155; vgl. deren Indices: Eque in foresta. Verf. meint equae indomitae = siluestres (nicht eine Rasse wilder Pferde); sie stehen in Angelsächs. Urkunden und dem Domesday: Earle Landchar. 222; Napier and Stevenson Crawford char. 130; Eyton Domesday stud. I 45. Ferner hält Rievaulx im 12. Jh. neben Rindern 60 matres equas cum nutrimento suo per forestam und faldas ad equos illaqueandos; Cart. Rieval. 157. 67

The Pipe rolls know studs in the forest from 1155; cf. their indexes: Eque in foresta. The author means equae indomitae = siluestres (not a breed of wild horses); they occur in Anglo-Saxon charters and in Domesday: Earle, Landchar. 222; Napier and Stevenson, Crawford char. 130; Eyton, Domesday stud. I 45. Further, Rievaulx in the 12th century keeps, besides cattle, 60 matres equas cum nutrimento suo per forestam and faldas ad equos illaqueandos; Cart. Rieval. 157. 67
f:c: tauri silvestres in Hertfordshire im 11. Jh. bei Mat. Paris, Gesta abb. S. Alb. I 40; vgl. Harting British animals extinct 220; und noch im 12. Jh. nahe London: Will. f. Steph. Descr. London. 6. Stellen späterer Zeit z. B. Mätzner s. v. bugle

tauri silvestres in Hertfordshire in the 11th century in Mat. Paris, Gesta abb. S. Alb. I 40; cf. Harting, British animals extinct 220; and still in the 12th century near London: Will. f. Steph., Descr. London. 6. Passages of later date e.g. Mätzner s. v. bugle

diffs: Print reads 'cure mediocrium'; our text has 'curo' (error, should be 'cure').

text: Uulpes{f:d} et lupi nec foreste nec{8} ueneris habentur, et proinde eorum interfectio{f:e} nulli emendationi subiacet{9}; si tamen infra limites occiduntur, fractio{f:f} sit regalis chacee{10} et{11} mitius emendetur.

f:d: vgl. lupos et uulpes et alias huiusmodi nociuas bestias; Cartul. de Novo Monast. 79. Doch verlieh Richard I. Fuchsjagd im Forst als Privileg; Fisher Forest of Essex 8. Den Wolf vertilgt die Krone seit dem 10. Jh., um 1178 luporum comprehensores besoldend (Dial. scacc. II 6; vgl. Hughes p. 216); vgl. Freeman Norm. conq. IV 608; Strutt ed. Hone Sports p. 19; Hn 90, 2; Cal. of Patent rolls 1272—81 p. 435; Turner p. xiii

cf. lupos et uulpes et alias huiusmodi nociuas bestias; Cartul. de Novo Monast. 79. But Richard I granted fox-hunting in the forest as a privilege; Fisher, Forest of Essex 8. The Crown exterminates the wolf from the 10th century on, paying luporum comprehensores around 1178 (Dial. scacc. II 6; cf. Hughes p. 216); cf. Freeman, Norm. conq. IV 608; Strutt ed. Hone, Sports p. 19; Hn 90, 2; Cal. of Patent rolls 1272–81 p. 435; Turner p. xiii

text: Aper{f:g} uero, quanquam foreste sit, nullatenus tamen{12} animal ueneris haberi est{13} assuetus.

f:g: Eber werden schon im 13. Jh. selten; Turner p. xii. Wilhelm I. schon stellte den Hirsch über, den Hasen unter den Eber; Ann. Anglosax. a. 1086
Boars become rare already in the 13th century; Turner p. xii. William I already set the hart above the boar and the hare below it; Ann. Anglosax. a. 1086

text: Bosco nec subbosco{f:h} nostro sine licentia{14} primariorum{f:i} foreste nemo manum apponat; quodsi quis fecerit, reus sit fractionis{f:f} regalis chacee.

f:h: Unterholz, jedoch mit Ausnahme des kleinen crimen uiridis 21, 2. Doch meint Verf. nur Wald innerhalb der foresta, nicht etwa auf sonstiger Königsdomäne
Underwood, but with the exception of the minor crimen uiridis, 21, 2. But the author means only woodland within the foresta, not on other royal demesne
f:i: per uisum custodum forestæ Dial. scacc. I 11; forestariorum et uiridariorum Assisa a. 1198, also leichter, wie Anm. r
per uisum custodum forestæ, Dial. scacc. I 11; forestariorum et uiridariorum, Assisa a. 1198, thus more lenient, like note r

diffs: Mark {f:f} (after fractionis) repeats note f of clause 27,2.

text: Si quis uero ilicem{f:k}, aut arborem aliquam{15} que uictum feris suppeditat, sciderit, preter fractionem{f:f} regalis chacee emendet regi uiginti solidos{16}.

f:k: das Fällen fruchttragender Bäume bestrafen auch andere Germanen strenger; Wilda Strafrecht 934. Sogar wo der Grundeigenthümer anderes Holz im Königsforst fällen darf, bleibt die Eiche geschützt; Turner Sel. pleas p. lxxiij. Die reguarda forestae seit Heinrich II. notiren unumquemque ceppum de quercu uel fago; Rog. Hov. II 243, wiederholt a. 1229 ed. Shirley Royal letters I 347

Other Germanic peoples too punish the felling of fruit-bearing trees more severely; Wilda, Strafrecht 934. Even where the landowner may fell other wood in the royal forest, the oak remains protected; Turner, Sel. pleas p. lxxiij. The reguarda forestae from Henry II on record unumquemque ceppum de quercu uel fago; Rog. Hov. II 243, repeated a. 1229, ed. Shirley, Royal letters I 347

diffs: Mark {f:f} (after fractionem) repeats note f of clause 27,2.

text: Uolo ut omnis liberalis{f:l}{17} homo pro libito suo habeat uenerem siue uiridem in{f:m} planis suis super sua{18}, sine{f:n} chacea tamen; et deuitent{19} omnes meam, ubicunque eam habere uoluero.

f:l: wie 26q adelsfreundlich, giebt Verf. Cnuts allgemeine Erlaubniss mit dem Rechte, Jaghunde zu halten, dem Adel allein
Favouring the nobility, as in 26 note q, the author gives Cnut's general permission, together with the right to keep hunting dogs, to the nobility alone
f:m: Verf. lässt siluis aus, offenbar will er die Jagdbefugniss des Unterthanen auch geographisch beschränken
The author omits siluis; evidently he wants to restrict the subject's hunting right geographically as well
f:n: ohne das Recht des Jagens missversteht Coke IV Inst. 320; Verf. meint, wie 21, 2r, ausserhalb des umhegten Jagdreviers; denn sine, wie afrz. sens und mhd. ohne, heisst öfter ausgenommen

Coke IV Inst. 320 misunderstands it as 'without the right of hunting'; the author means, as in 21, 2 note r, 'outside the enclosed hunting ground'; for sine, like Old French sens and Middle High German ohne, often means 'except'
19: dimittet omnia mea u. ea h. Cii
dimittet omnia mea u. ea h. Cii

text: Nullus mediocris{f:l} habebit nec custodiet canes, quos Angli greihounds{f:p}{20} appellant.

f:p: -nde in zwei Hss., ist später Singular mit stummem -e. Das Compositum ist Lehnwort vom Nord. greyhundr 'Hündin'; doch heisst auch grey allein dasselbe. Für Lyes grighund scheint einzige Quelle Wright-Wülker Vocab. 276, 3. Falsche Etymologie um 1310 s. o. S. 367*. Ass. de foresta Heinrichs II. 14 setzt dafür mastiui

-nde in two MSS is a later singular with mute -e. The compound is a loanword from Norse greyhundr 'bitch'; but grey alone also means the same. For Lye's grighund the only source seems to be Wright-Wülker, Vocab. 276, 3. False etymology around 1310, see above p. 367*. Henry II's Ass. de foresta 14 has mastiui instead
20: greyhounde dicunt instead of g. a. St Cii

text: Liberali uero, dum genuscissio{f:q}{21} eorum facta fuerit coram{f:r} primario foreste, licebit; aut sine genuscissione{22}, dum remoti sunt{5} a limitibus foreste per decem miliaria{23}; quanto{24} uero propius{25} uenerint, emendet quodlibet miliare{26} uno solido.

f:q: die Einführung der Lähmung der Hunde schreibt Ordric XI (ed. Le Prévost IV 238) Heinrich dem I. zu, wofür auch Galfr. Monm. VII 3 spricht; sie heisst misera Hn 17, besteht vor 1135 laut vieler Quellen, u. a. Blount Tenures ed. Hazlitt 305, wo das Lähmen impediare heisst. Technisch ist später expeditacio (so Henr. II Ass. de for. 14), laut Charta de for. a. 1217, 6 vor 1154 gebräuchlich. Auch private Jagdbesitzer übten sie: Umfravil schenkt 1181 Newminster partem forestæ, ita quod canes pede carebunt; Cart. de Novo-Monast. (Surtees soc.) p. 74. Bischof Hugo von Durham erlaubt: pedes canum eorum non sint truncati; hinter Boldon buke (Surtees soc.) p. xlvi

Ordric XI (ed. Le Prévost IV 238) attributes the introduction of the lawing (lamming) of dogs to Henry I, which Galfr. Monm. VII 3 also supports; it is called misera in Hn 17, and exists before 1135 according to many sources, among others Blount, Tenures, ed. Hazlitt 305, where the laming is called impediare. Later the technical term is expeditacio (so Henr. II Ass. de for. 14), in use before 1154 according to the Charta de for. a. 1217, 6. Private holders of hunting rights practised it too: in 1181 Umfravil gives Newminster partem forestæ, ita quod canes pede carebunt; Cart. de Novo-Monast. (Surtees soc.) p. 74. Bishop Hugh of Durham permits: pedes canum eorum non sint truncati; at the end of Boldon buke (Surtees soc.) p. xlvi
f:r: die Lähmung (in uicinio siluarum laut Ordric) geschah im 12. Jh. vor den Förstern, nicht den Forstrichtern
The laming (in uicinio siluarum according to Ordric) took place in the 12th century before the foresters, not the forest judges
